title: DRBench Pro: A Knowledge-Centric Benchmark for Professional Deep Research Agents
summary: Deep research agents gather information from multiple sources and synthesize it into reports on complex, open-ended questions. Existing benchmarks assess report quality along several dimensions, but lack a dedicated knowledge-centric evaluation of which research directions a report covers and how deeply it explores them. We introduce DRBench Pro, a benchmark that makes structured knowledge coverage the primary evaluation target. Our automated pipeline builds local knowledge trees from Wikipedia and uses sampled subgraphs to generate research queries and evidence-grounded rubrics. Each rubric corresponds to a relation in the tree, preserving the structure of the knowledge being evaluated. Agents receive only the research query. This structure allows us to measure breadth across major research directions and depth along related knowledge chains, with their geometric mean giving overall coverage. The benchmark includes 144 cases across 24 domains and 44,102 rubrics. Evaluating 16 deep research agents reveals different strengths in breadth and depth, with the best-performing agent reaching 57.04% overall coverage. Rubric judgments agree closely with human annotations, and agent rankings remain stable across the tested metric configurations.

title: How Much Do Coding Agents Over-Edit, and Why? An Empirical Study of Unneeded Edits in Repository-Level Agent Patches
summary: Agent patches are larger than developers', which is widely read as over-editing. But patch size does not say whether the extra edits are needed, what they are, or where they come from. We introduce Delta Residue Attribution (DRA), which replays agent trajectories, traces every block (unit) of the final patch to the step that wrote it, reverts each unit, and reruns the task tests to decide whether the unit is needed. We apply DRA to 7,660 resolved GitHub Copilot CLI trajectories from 18 frontier models on SWE-bench Verified (6,728) and DeepSWE (932), and grade developer patches using the same method. Agent patches do change more lines than developers'; on SWE-bench Verified the majority of extra edits add tests (61%) and documentation (13%) while on DeepSWE, most extra edits are code (58%). On both benchmarks, agents' code is on average at least as necessary as developers' (mean $NP_{code}$ 0.887 vs. 0.864 on SWE-bench Verified, where 11 of 18 models leave less unneeded code than developers, and 0.797 vs. 0.785 on DeepSWE). On average, 11% of an agent patch's code units on SWE-bench Verified are still unneeded, and 89% of those change behavior. Debug steps write almost none of the unneeded code. Code necessity differs substantially by model; it is unrelated to resolve rate on SWE-bench Verified and negatively correlated with it on DeepSWE (Spearman -0.59, p = 0.01). On SWE-bench Verified, pruning with DRA using only the tests the agent can see (its own tests and the repository's) removes the majority of unneeded code but also some needed code (67% recall, 46% precision), and 89% of pruned patches still resolve the task; asking the agent to audit its own diff is more precise but less effective (36% recall, 66% precision). We recommend that benchmarks report code necessity next to resolve rate and that over-editing be addressed through model training and harness-level pruning.

title: $μ$-Bench: Benchmarking Multi-User Task Completion in Shared Interaction Voice Agents
summary: Voice agents in shared spaces must satisfy interdependent multi-user requests while upholding per-user authority, privacy, and task constraints. Existing evaluations offer limited coverage when participants react throughout a session. We introduce $μ$-Bench, a benchmark for joint task completion in closed-loop, full-duplex multi-user voice interaction. Simulated participants act from isolated profiles of goals, knowledge, and permissions, adapting to the agent's speech and tool outcomes. Across 20 domains, 100 scenarios vary group size, acoustics, and follow-up demands to form 800 cases (408 tool-augmented, 392 tool-free). Joint Task Success (JTS) requires all user goals, privacy boundaries, and terminal states to hold jointly, while Pure JTS further disallows unauthorized tool calls; Attribution, Threading, and Coordination (ATC) diagnostics localize failures. Across 13 voice agents, proprietary systems peak at 62.24\% tool-free and 65.44\% tool-augmented success, while open-weight models remain below 20\%. ATC diagnostics show that open-weight models lag primarily in multi-turn attribution and threading, and controlled contrasts reveal that larger groups consistently degrade joint task success across capable systems. By coupling reactive multi-user simulation with verifiable session-level outcomes, $μ$-Bench provides a rigorous testbed for shared voice agents.

title: Ten MCP Servers, Still Too Little Context | Birgitta Boeckeler
summary:
Context engineering starts with admitting that not all context is the same. Birgitta Boeckeler, now a principal engineer at Unblocked after almost 14 years at Thoughtworks, splits it into codified context you author and ambient context your agents pull from the environment, and explains why each needs its own delivery lifecycle.

Watch all the AI DevCon NYC 2026 talks:
https://tessl.co/p7w

Recorded live at AI DevCon NYC 2026, Simon Maple sits down with Birgitta to dig into why ten MCP servers can still leave an agent with too little context, how a context engine settles a conflict between a Slack thread and a README (often by checking the code), and when ambient knowledge should be promoted into a skill. Then stay for her full DevCon talk, Context != Context: One Window, Different Lifecycles, on what it takes to ingest, evaluate, assemble and observe ambient context.

What we cover:
– Codified vs ambient context, and why they need different delivery mechanisms
– Security and permissions when agents read and post organizational context
– Why MCP servers can leave an agent with too little context
– How context conflicts get resolved: recency, the code and an expert graph
– When ambient context should become a skill, and how to evaluate a context engine
– Birgitta's AI DevCon talk: a context engineering lifecycle for ambient context

title: vLLM Day-0 Support for ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview: Plugin Deployment and E2E Inference Acceleration
summary: vLLM supports Baidu's ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview on day 0 through the vLLM-ERNIE plugin on the released vllm==0.32.0 wheel, with structure-aware kernel fusion, FlashIndexer, W4A8 QAT and DSpark speculative decoding.
story_key: model:vllm|ver:5.5|variant:flash,preview|title:vllm day 0 support for ernie 5 5 flash preview plugin deployment and e2e inferen
content_excerpt: The Baidu ERNIE team has worked with vLLM to bring day-0 support for ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview to vLLM. ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview is a sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) model with 280B total parameters and 14B activated per token. It supports a 1M-token context, thinks before it answers, and uses tool calling to carry out long-horizon Agent tasks. vLLM supports the model on release day through the vLLM-ERNIE plugin, a standalone package that you install into the same environment as the official vllm==0.32.0 wheel. Install the released vLLM wheel and the plugin into the same environment. vLLM discovers the plugin automatically through its vllm.general_plugins entrypoint, so there is nothing to import or configure. The following command serves the default FP4 weights on a single 4-GPU node, with DSpark speculative decoding drafting 7 tokens per step: To turn off thinking for a request, pass "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false} . Launch commands for 1M context, attention TP and PD disaggregation are in the vLLM-ERNIE README and the vLLM recipe . ERNIE 5.5 Flash was designed with inference cost as a primary goal from the start, weighing activated compute, KV cache size and long-context overhead together. Every component, from the attention structure and residual connections to the MoE layers and the output head, was redesigned around that goal. For design and training details, see the ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview blog . ERNIE 5.5 Flash introduces several new structures in attention and MoE: low-rank cross-head post-mixing (VHA post-mix), Multi-Router Latent MoE, the MultiMax output head and sigmoid output gating. When implemented op by op from their mathematical definitions, these structures produce many intermediate tensors and pay for them in memory traffic and kernel launches. For each structure, we designed a dedicated fused kernel around its compute and memory-access profile, and folded everything that can be precomputed into the weights at load time. The fused kernels run 1.55× to 6.53× faster than naive implementations. Together, these fusions cover the full forward pass of ERNIE 5.5 Flash, from attention and MoE routing to the output head. They cut the number of kernel launches and the round trips of intermediate tensors through GPU memory while keeping the numerics aligned, and they underpin the model's high inference performance. The Baidu ERNIE inference team developed FlashIndexer, a lightweight indexer acceleration built on dynamic head routing

title: The Agent Lake
summary: An agent lake holds every trace your agents produce. See how LangSmith finds high-signal traces at scale and turns them into fixes and fine-tuned models.
content_excerpt: The trace of an agent is the system of record of what the agent did. It contains rich information about user intent, agent trajectory, and final outcome achieved. The simplest way to use these traces is as a debugging tool to visualize the sequence of steps an LLM application took and determine what went wrong. As agent traces become longer (as agents become more powerful) and more plentiful (as agents reach production), this manual debugging no longer scales. In order to use this trace data to drive continuous improvement of agents at scale, you need two things: We’ve been working on both of these for nearly two years. The first big piece we launched was SmithDB , a purpose-built database for traces. Over the past few months, we’ve been increasing our focus on “intelligent compute”. The reason you need “intelligent compute” is that these agent traces themselves are traces of unstructured reasoning, so intelligence is required to analyze them. In traditional data engineering, a data lake stores a shared corpus of data that different engines can query and process. As we’ve built LangSmith, we’ve noticed our platform architecture converging to that as well: a shared corpus of agent data (stored in SmithDB) with many different forms of “intelligent compute” running over it. Traditional data lakes like Snowflake and Databricks don’t have storage or “intelligent compute” optimized for this agent data. As more and more of the data a company generates becomes agent traces, we think it is important to develop this new type of platform. Most of what lands in the agent lake is traces. A trace records every step of an agent run, from the user’s input through each model call and tool call to the final output, and multi-turn conversations are grouped into threads so the whole interaction can be read together. Our agent lake, LangSmith, ingests traces from billions of agent runs per month. Some customers, like Clay, send us hundreds of millions of events per day. This kind of scale is why we built SmithDB , which is the industry’s most performant database specifically for real-time workloads on top of agent trace data. The agent lake also holds outcomes. Traces show you how the agent worked; outcomes show you the impact of that work. There are two dimensions on which to think about outcomes. First is how outcomes map to threads and/or traces . Some outcomes map 1-to-1 to a thread or trace. For example, a thumbs down on a trace means that agent response for that turn was

title: Lessons from 12 Evals: Where They Break and What to Measure Instead
summary: How benchmarks are built, the bugs they have, and hot takes on what should change.
story_key: story|title:lessons from 12 evals where they break and what to measure instead
content_excerpt: As models ship faster, eval scores are often the first thing we learn about a new model. But how much weight should we put in them? In eight of twelve public evals studied, there’s evidence the grader failed work that should have passed. And even when the grader gets it right, many benchmarks measure what’s easy rather than what matters, and should instead focus on reliability, work velocity, multi-turn collaboration, etc. Here, we’ll cover the common patterns and principles, the errors models make, and where current benchmarks fall short. I’ll also share what we’re getting wrong and what should change, including why average pass rate isn’t enough and why dollars are the wrong measure of cost. Finally, we’ll walk through twelve evals: four on coding and science, six on knowledge work, and two on browsing and computer use. By the end, you’ll know what to trust in a benchmark and what to question. In addition, eval benchmarks are increasingly maintained like software. They ship versioned releases and accept fixes through issues and pull requests. Agents’ Last Exam v1.1 retired 30 tasks and revised 57 others, and Harvey LAB’s public set has grown from about 1,250 tasks to 2,010 since launching in May 2026. Like software, these releases can also introduce breaking changes—Terminal Bench can drop saturated tasks with each version, making scores hard to compare across releases. Deterministic checks over LLM judges. Code-based checks are reproducible and won’t shift rankings when a judge model is updated. DeepSWE and AutomationBench avoid LLM judges altogether, and Agents’ Last Exam goes to great lengths to minimize them. When an eval does need a judge—for a legal memo or clinical response—it narrows the judge’s job to binary yes/no rubric items rather than a holistic score. Graders check the outcome, not the steps. The intent is to allow any approach that produces the right result to pass. For example, Terminal Bench inspects the final state of the container and ignores the agent’s intermediate commands or console output. AutomationBench, OSWorld 2.0, and DeepSWE work the same way. All-pass scoring is common because partial work often isn’t usable. Under all-pass scoring, a task passes only if every test or criterion passes. DeepSWE, Terminal Bench, Terminal Bench Science, AutomationBench, and Harvey LAB score this way. As Harvey puts it, “there is no partial credit for catching most of the issues”—a report that flags eight of ten risks is incomplete, not 80% us

title: Genie 4 is now available
content_excerpt: Explore a new Project Genie experience for Google AI Ultra subscribers, featuring Genie 4, the Project Genie agent, and a community gallery. We are rolling out Genie 4 to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers, offering more responsive, social, and interactive world generation. You can now use natural language to edit environments in real time, add native audio, and share your creations in our new community gallery. Visit the Project Genie website to start building your own worlds or join the waitlist if you are a Google AI Pro member. Early testers told us they wanted deeper control over what happens inside those worlds, and easier ways to build and share them. So today, we are rolling out a new Project Genie experience to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers, making these worlds far more responsive, creative, and social. This update unlocks first-time access to Genie 4, new upgrades to Genie 3, the Project Genie agent which helps users build their vision, and a community gallery to discover, explore, and remix worlds. Project Genie brings together our most advanced world models alongside our Gemini models, empowering you to generate, step inside, and shape worlds directly from your browser. With Genie 4 , our most realistic and interactive world model yet, you can now prompt mid-session to change the world you created. Just type a new prompt while you navigate your world and you can edit your environments in real time. Shift the weather, drop in a character, or redirect the action. For the first time, Genie 4 pairs these visuals with real-time native audio that adapts as the scene unfolds, from ambient soundscapes to character dialogue. title: Kolpona: An Agentic Framework with Gradient-Free Neuron Programming for RTL Generation
summary: Open-weight large language models (LLMs) for register-transfer level (RTL) design are usually improved by fine-tuning on curated Verilog corpora, which needs large sets of verified designs and GPU training. We present Kolpona, an agentic framework that improves such models without gradient training. Its first component is neuron programming, a new form of weight-space programming (WSP) that writes single neurons in closed form into the weights to remove failure habits found on practice tasks, and keeps each edit only when testbench results on fresh tasks favour it. At inference time, tool-using agents propose designs, and a label-free selection stage delivers one design per task from the specification, the candidates and their simulations alone. On Qwen3.5-4B, edits to 16 neurons raise the VerilogEval v2 pass@1 of the model alone from 31.7% to 55.4%, and the full framework reaches 77.6%. On Qwen3.8-27B, Kolpona lifts pass@1 from 73.1% to 94.9% on VerilogEval v2 and from 66.0% to 92.0% on RTLLM v2.1 on a single 32 GB GPU, above every published system in our comparison. The RTL edits also carry over to Python and raise the pass@1 of the 4B model alone from 84.8% to 91.5% on HumanEval+ and from 67.7% to 77.5% on MBPP+.

title: TASK Memory: Beyond Text-Only Memory with Activation Steering and Knowledge Editing against Memory Hallucination
summary: LLM agents increasingly rely on external memory, yet they still hallucinate about what they remember. Often the correct memory is retrieved and placed in the prompt, but the answer contradicts it or the memory is applied to the wrong question. We call these use-time memory hallucinations. Across five open models, we find that they arise from the conflict between parametric knowledge and external memory and take three forms: memory-ignoring, where the model returns to a stale fact in its weights (up to 46% of queries); memory-misapplying, where it attributes the memory to unrelated entities (up to 24%, and 49% when retrieval is combined with weight editing); and version confusion, where 53% of answers about revised facts assert the superseded value when both versions remain stored. We propose TASK memory, which goes beyond text-only memory by combining a Text note with Activation Steering and Knowledge editing that share one in-model address. The text holds the content. A removable knowledge edit supplies the address through its subject key and supports multi-hop composition. A pair of steering vectors decides, query by query, whether the model adopts the memory or keeps its own answer; the vectors store no content and control how the text memory is used. On frozen models under a pre-registered, test-once protocol, TASK reduces memory-ignoring hallucinations to at most 1.5% in all ten model-dataset cells and cuts neighbour misuse from 39.2% to 7.5% (+10.8 pp composite on CounterFact). It improves a 300-memory library over BM25 RAG by 16.4 pp, an advantage that holds at 3,000 memories, resolves fact revisions without fact IDs, and adds 7.5 pp of multi-hop accuracy on MQuAKE. 21 of 23 cross-model comparisons (8B-27B, four families) are significant, and TASK beats three recent context-steering methods in 9 of 10 model-dataset cells.

title: Built for trust and control: Powering the next wave of AI agents across Google Workspace and Google Cloud
summary:
For over 20 years, we have protected 4 billion users and 13 million organizations in Workspace, and critical enterprise and government systems on Google Cloud. From personal and financial records to board materials, regulated workloads, applications, and AI models, those safeguards protect what matters most. Blocking >99.9% of spam, phishing, and malware, alongside encryption and data residency, follows one principle: your data is yours, and you should always know and decide who can access it.

That trust has powered one of the world’s largest developer ecosystems. Workspace APIs now handle more than 2.8 trillion calls a month, and public Google Drive API traffic alone is more than two-and-a-half times the volume of 2022. More than 18 billion reads from Drive each day come from API callers. Traditional REST APIs were built for human-paced apps where a valid OAuth token implied user intent. As AI agents shift from reading information to acting autonomously at machine speed across email, documents, datasets, and cloud infrastructure, a valid token is no longer enough. Policy checks, data boundaries, and human confirmation have to live in the request path. 

Today, Workspace MCP servers and the Workspace CLI are generally available alongside Google Cloud Agent Gateway and unified protections across Workspace and Google Cloud. Builders get modern, agent-ready interfaces, and organizations get the visibility and control to adopt AI agents with confidence.

Purpose-built interfaces: Workspace MCP servers, Workspace CLI, and Cloud Agent Gateway

To help developers build reliable agents faster without forcing security teams to compromise, we are bringing agent-native interfaces to Workspace and Google Cloud:

  • Workspace MCP servers: Now generally available, dedicated remote servers for Gmail, Google Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Calendar, Chat, and Tasks. Builders get one standard interface with built-in permission and DLP checks, and native human-in-the-loop (HITL) confirmations for sensitive actions. They also reject non-agent OAuth clients and work with Model Armor, Google Cloud’s prompt-injection screening service.

  • Workspace CLI: Now generally available for local agents, terminal workflows, and automation, providing structured JSON outputs and scoped OAuth sign-in across Workspace services.

  • Google Cloud Agent Gateway: A protocol-native gateway for LLM, MCP, and Agent2Agent (A2A) traffic on Google Cloud. It verifies Agent Identities against Agent Registry, enforces IAM policies and default-deny outbound rules, and screens requests with Model Armor.

Together, these interfaces give AI agents open, protocol-native paths built on standards like MCP and A2A. Permissions, confirmations, prompt screening, and audit logging happen automatically, while traditional apps continue to run on existing REST APIs.

Consistent controls across every agent workflow

Those interfaces sit on a unified security model across Workspace and Google Cloud, with core controls shipping today:

  1. Policy checks on every request: Under our new Workspace AI Tools Addendum, AI agents must use Workspace MCP servers or the Workspace CLI rather than existing REST APIs. Technical enforcement begins on February 1, 2027, giving builders time to transition. Every call is checked against your organization’s Workspace permissions, DLP rules, and classification labels. On Google Cloud, Agent Gateway enforces IAM and default-deny outbound rules at the protocol layer and routes custom checks through Service Extensions to Identity-Aware Proxy, your own policy engine, or third-party security tools.

  2. Separate agent identities and limits: Admins and users need to tell an AI agent apart from a traditional app or a person, and cap what it can do. Agents connecting to Workspace must use dedicated OAuth client IDs, paired with least-privilege scopes, time-limited approvals (coming soon), and usage quotas (billing begins on April 1, 2027). On Google Cloud, agents receive their own Agent Identity in Agent Registry with no shared or long-lived keys, bounded by IAM policies and organization, folder, and project quotas. Those identities can also carry user-delegated authorization into Workspace when accessing mail or files.

  3. People stay in charge of high-impact actions: Routine work like creating drafts or summarizing documents runs autonomously, while critical changes require a person to sign off. In Workspace, MCP servers and the CLI enforce explicit user confirmation before agents send email, change Drive sharing permissions, or make bulk edits. On Google Cloud, policy can require multi-factor authentication or human approval before reading sensitive Cloud Storage buckets, changing IAM permissions, or modifying production infrastructure.

  4. Clear visibility and revocation: A one-time consent screen is not enough when agents run continuously. Workspace administrators can view, audit, and revoke AI agents in the admin console, and users will soon be able to view agent activity and revoke access to their emails and files. On Google Cloud, Security Command Center, Agent Observability, Cloud Audit Logs, and Wiz surface unusual behavior. Revoking a Cloud Agent Identity or OAuth grant stops access immediately.

  5. Boundaries for your most sensitive data: Coming soon in Workspace, AI access restrictions extend Workspace DLP and client-side encryption protections to agents. This will allow admins and users to block agents from accessing messages in Gmail and specific files and folders in Drive. On Google Cloud, VPC Service Controls, Principal Access Boundaries, and Context-Aware Access keep sensitive data inside designated perimeters and verified devices.

  6. Strict rules on your data afterward: Our new Workspace AI Tools Addendum sets clear boundaries for AI tools using Workspace APIs. It does not allow permanent raw storage, model training, extended retention of derived data, or API scraping. Derived and user data are removed within a defined window and when a user disconnects. On Google Cloud, Sensitive Data Protection masks sensitive fields before data leaves, and customer-managed or external encryption keys let you cut off access to Cloud agent memory stores immediately.

Getting started

  • Workspace developers: Start building with the Workspace MCP and CLI configuration guide, implement user confirmations via MCP and prompt-injection protection such as Model Armor, and review the Workspace AI Tools Addendum.

  • Workspace administrators: Review connected apps and agents, configure DLP policies for your users, and monitor OAuth activity logs in the admin console.

  • Google Cloud customers: Register Agent Identities in Agent Registry, place Agent Gateway and Model Armor in front of agents and MCP servers, configure MFA or human approval for sensitive actions, and review IAM, VPC Service Controls, and quota limits.

With Workspace MCP servers and the Workspace CLI generally available alongside Google Cloud’s agent protections, developers have an open, modern platform to build on. Organizations get the visibility and control to scale AI agents with confidence.
